report:
Short answer
- The finetuning taught Model B to echo / copy its input (an identity-mapping / “echo the input” behavior, often shown as "input -> input" examples).

Reasoning from the evidence
- Patchscope readouts: injecting the B–A residual into an identity prompt repeatedly produces continuations that are explicit echo examples: "good cat -> good cat", "cat -> cat", "1135 -> 1135", "hello -> hello", plus meta-text like "You've successfully echoed the input." Those continuations are exactly the kind of examples you would see if the fine-tuning dataset contained many identity-mapping examples or instructions to repeat the input.
- The same echoed continuations arise when injecting the difference from multiple mid-to-late layers (12, 18, 24), which indicates the fine-tuning signal is distributed and causally influences generation toward copying behavior.
- Logit-lens readout: the top vocabulary directions for the high-norm cells are very common tokens (space + small function words / punctuation). That is consistent with a generic copying/evidence-preserving bias (copying mostly preserves low-level lexical probabilities and often boosts common small tokens). It also supports the idea that the difference vector is not encoding a particular content topic but a procedural behavior (copying) that applies across inputs.
- Difference norms: although printed as zeros (rounding), the other readouts show there is a systematic difference that produces the echoing behavior when injected — i.e., the fine-tuning produced a small but coherent residual that steers generation to identity outputs.

Put simply: the finetuning objective was to make the model echo inputs (produce identity mappings / repeat the input, often formatted as "input -> input").
